item.title: Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
item.description:
Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria NevesByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:22 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.
Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.
Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.
In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.
The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.
Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.
Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.
Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.

item.title: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talksByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:13 AM
MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.
The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.
Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.
The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.
The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”

item.title: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
item.description:
Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
Congo’s Ebola outbreak remains out of control six months after it was announced, with more than 11,000 cases recorded and nearly half proving fatalByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:02 AM
BUNIA, Congo -- Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities’ ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.

item.title: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
item.description:
Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
Millions of Argentines have turned out to see Pope Leo XIV — and the words that moved them most often belonged to his predecessor, and their compatriot, FrancisByISABEL DEBRE Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:00 AM
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.
Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week's adulation.
Francis’ fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.
“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”
Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’ face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth," declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo's welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.

item.title: Africa is charting a different road to electric mobility with motorbikes and versatile 3-wheelers
item.description:
Africa is charting a different road to electric mobility with motorbikes and versatile 3-wheelers
In Africa, the electric vehicle transition is taking a different route from wealthier markets, with motorcycles and three-wheelers emerging as practical alternatives to passenger carsByFARAI MUTSAKA Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 11:54 PM
Share
HARARE, Zimbabwe -- The electric vehicle revolution in Zimbabwe began on rural dirt paths. Three-wheeled vehicles carried cabbages to markets, women farmers to their fields and patients to clinics in communities where transport has long been scarce.
For farmer Agefi Mutambo, the owner of an electric three-wheeler since 2021, it has transformed her business and family.
Before, she walked seven to 10 kilometers (4.3 to 6.2 miles) balancing a 20-kilogram (44-pound) bucket of tomatoes on her head that she sold for $6.
“The money wasn't even enough for food. I would do a single trip a day, arrive at the market late and the produce would no longer be as fresh,” the 56-year-old said.
Now she makes two to three deliveries a week transporting 300 kilograms (661 pounds) of produce on each trip, grossing roughly $80 a trip supplying schools and clinics. She also ferries neighbors to hospital, sometimes at midnight for a woman in labor.
“When my battery is low, I simply swap it for $4, and I am back on the road,” she said.
Mutambo is among dozens of rural women entrepreneurs in Zimbabwe whose lives have been transformed by electric tricycles introduced by local social enterprise Mobility for Africa in 2019.
The company introduced the solar-charged tricycles, powered by lithium-ion batteries, mainly for rural women, under a lease-to-own scheme costing about $30 a week. Called “Hamba,” meaning “go” in the local Ndebele language, the vehicles can carry loads of over 400 kilograms (880 pounds) and travel about 100 kilometers (62 miles) on a single charge. item.title: Mayan ceremony in Guatemala honors Nobel winner Miguel Ángel Asturias
item.description:
Mayan ceremony in Guatemala honors Nobel winner Miguel Ángel Asturias
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchú Tum attended the ritual.BySONIA PÉREZ D. Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 5:36 PM
GUATEMALA CITY, Guatemala -- A Mayan ceremony held Saturday at an archaeological site in Guatemala’s capital paid tribute to Nobel Prize-winning author Miguel Ángel Asturias, whose ashes returned to his Central American country this week after decades abroad.
The ritual at the Kaminal Juyú site brought together the writer’s family and special guests, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchú Tum. The altar was adorned for the ceremony with white, purple, red and yellow flowers, representing the four cardinal directions. There were also candles, incense and cinnamon.
Menchú approached the 32-kilogram (70-pound) green jade urn that holds Asturias’ ashes before the ritual, placing her hands upon it. She then offered a prayer, spoke to the urn and kissed it.
“Today, we are here, honored by the eternal presence of Don Miguel Ángel Asturias, not only in Guatemala, but throughout the world,” she said. She later encouraged the Guatemalan people to keep the writer’s memory alive by reading his works.
The remains of Asturias arrived in Guatemala on Thursday from France, where the writer had been buried following his death in exile in 1974. Asturias died of cancer in Madrid seven years after receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature.
His work is considered a precursor to Magical Realism and a key factor in the boom of Latin American literature during the 1960s and 1970s.
He went into exile after a 1954 coup led by Gen. Carlos Castillo Armas, who revoked his passport and stripped him of his Guatemalan citizenship, labeling him a communist. Asturias' final visit to Guatemala took place in 1966. By then, the country was already gripped by violence and repression, fueled by a war between the army and guerrilla forces.

item.title: Panamanian authorities investigate bombing attack on investigative reporter's home
item.description:
Panamanian authorities investigate bombing attack on investigative reporter's home
Authorities in Panama are investigating a bombing attack on the home of an investigative journalistByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 4:21 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PANAMA CITY, Panama -- A bombing attack Saturday on the home of an investigative reporter in Panama was being investigated by authorities, the newspaper “La Prensa” reported.
No one was injured in the attack targeting journalist Rolando Rodríguez, according to “La Prensa,” which publishes his work.
The Attorney General’s Office of Panama said authorities were investigating a possible case of arson but said the probe may be expanded if other crimes are uncovered.
“While this was an attack on my life and the lives of my family, I must say that it changes the rules of the game in Panama,” Rodríguez told reporters Saturday. “Because now, we are all potentially exposed to this kind of thing.”
Rodríguez is a veteran investigative journalist and columnist who has led or contributed to numerous investigations into alleged corruption and irregularities within Panama’s public sector, the judiciary and businesses.
“La Prensa” reported that the attack at Rodríguez's home came at a time when he was preparing to publish a piece implicating former officials from the administration of President José Raúl Mulino and a government contractor.

item.title: Hundreds of men lead protest to urge other men to help reduce violence against women
item.description:
Hundreds of men lead protest to urge other men to help reduce violence against women
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in the Swiss capital to denounce violence against womenByJAMEY KEATEN Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 2:22 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BERN, Switzerland -- Hundreds of men led a demonstration in the Swiss capital on Saturday to denounce misogyny and a plague of violence against women, insisting men need to take a bigger and more vocal role in fighting both.
The “Men against Violence against Women” rally outside parliament follows high and persistent concerns that expressions of misogyny are too present online among teenage boys and young men — and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.
It comes as some influencers on the fringe of the right-wing “manosphere” were emboldened after President Donald Trump'spresidential win in 2024 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.
Academics and advocacy groups, for the first time, have tried to map the extent of the movement in Switzerland.
A survey released in June by the University of Zurich and mencare, an umbrella group of Swiss men's and fathers' organizations, found half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 had expressed concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalized in society" and had a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity.”
The study pointed to the need for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence. The debate should start in schools.”
The Swiss government has been taking note: Justice Minister Beat Jans earlier this month attended a conference designed to raise awareness about the hazards of violent invective online against women.

item.title: At least 6 killed and 11 injured when bus overturns in southwestern Colombia
item.description:
At least 6 killed and 11 injured when bus overturns in southwestern Colombia
Police report that at least six people are dead and 11 injured after a bus overturned on a highway in southwestern ColombiaByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 2:04 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BOGOTA, Colombia -- A bus overturned Saturday on a highway in southwestern Colombia, killing at least six people and injuring 11, the National Police said.
A police report seen by The Associated Press said the driver may have briefly fallen asleep at the wheel, causing the incident.
Videos shared on social media showed emergency personnel assisting injured passengers and people crying next to the overturned bus on the Garzon–Neiva highway. The bus, which was headed to the capital, Bogota, was later removed from the road and traffic was restored.
The police report states authorities were still trying to determine the exact circumstances under which the bus overturned in the department of Huila, but they believe the driver may have experienced an episode of “microsleep" — falling asleep for a few seconds.

item.title: Bomb rips through Damascus suburb killing 2 including a child
item.description:
Bomb rips through Damascus suburb killing 2 including a child
The device placed inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital.ByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 1:43 PM
DAMASCUS, Syria -- An explosive device placed inside a car in a suburb of Syria's capital exploded Saturday evening, killing two people and wounding at least one, state TV and the Interior Ministry said.
The explosion took place in the southern Damascus suburb of Jaramana near a factory where batteries are produced, state TV said. It said two people were killed and two were wounded, without giving further details.
The Interior Ministry said the dead included a child, adding that one person was wounded. It said security forces cordoned off the area and started an investigation.

Several explosions have taken place in Damascus and its suburbs in recent months as the country’s security remains fragile nearly two years after five decades of Assad family rule ended in December 2024. Militants stormed the capital and removed then-President Bashar Assad from power.
Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority. The suburb has faced tensions between some members of the community and Sunni Muslim Syrians supportive of the country’s current Islamist-led government.
